'''''Pachysandra terminalis''''', the '''Japanese pachysandra''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PATE11|taxon=Pachysandra terminalis|accessdate=30 January 2016}}</ref> '''carpet box'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Japanese spurge''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the boxwood [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Buxaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to Japan, Korea and China and introduced to eastern North America.<ref>{{bonap|genus=Pachysandra|species=terminalis}}</ref> It is a slow-growing, spreading [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing to {{convert|10|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|60|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad, with alternate, simple, glossy [[leaf|leaves]], and creeping stems. The leaves may yellow in direct sunlight or in winter. When growing in a spreading mass of many plants, a dense cover is formed.

The flowers are white, borne above the foliage. In [[temperateness|temperate]] Northern Hemisphere sites they appear late in the month of March and throughout the month of April. The plant is very cold [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]].

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''terminalis'' means "ending", and refers to the clusters of leaves which appear at the end of the short stems.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Pachysandra terminalis'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], for use as a massed [[groundcover]], low grouped element, or accent plant in the ground. It is a suitable lower plant for [[container garden]]ing, and shaded or "northside" [[window box]]es. It takes about three years to establish a solid groundcover in suitable climates, when new plantings are spaced {{convert|6|-|12|in|cm|abbr=on|order=flip}} apart. It spreads by new stems sprouting from the spreading root system.

The plant prefers a moist and well-drained soil that is both acidic and rich.  A [[humus]] amended loam (acidic pH) [[soil]], with regular [[organic fertilizer]] applications and watering-rainfall is optimal. However, the plant is tolerant of neutral to slightly alkaline pH soils, and to periodic dryness, especially in humid and non-arid climates.

===Cultivars===
Numerous [[cultivars]] have been developed for garden use, of which 'Variegata'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Pachysandra terminalis'' 'Variegata'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/91844/Pachysandra-terminalis-Variegata-(v)/Details | access-date = 16 January 2021}}</ref> has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 71 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 14 April 2018}}</ref>

===Propagation===
''Pachysandra terminalis'' can be propagated by dividing and transplanting clumps, by rooting stem cuttings, or by removing seedlings that have grown through the spread of roots from the main flower.

==Invasiveness==
''Pachysandra terminalis'' is highly invasive in the United States and Canada.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.cfm?sub=3058#sources | title = Japanese pachysandra | date = 2018 | publisher = Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States | accessdate = 9 July 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://elibrary.dcnr.pa.gov/PDFProvider.ashx?action=PDFStream&docID=1738721&chksum=&revision=0&docName=Japanese+pachysandra&nativeExt=pdf&PromptToSave=False&Size=203340&ViewerMode=2&overlay=0 | title = Invasive Plants in Pennsylvania: Japanese Pachysandra (''Pachysandra terminalis'' Sieb. & Zucc.)  | date = 16 April 2012 | publisher = Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources | accessdate = 9 July 2026}}</ref> Brought to North America from Asia as an ornamental groundcover, it spreads aggressively via underground rhizomes. It forms dense, evergreen mats that expand across property lines, crowding out native species and altering forest ecosystems. There are many native groundcovers that can be substituted for Japanese pachysandra.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.inournature.ca/native-alternatives-to-invasive-plants#pachysandra | title = Native Alternatives to Invasive Plants in Ontario: Pachysandra (''Pachysandra terminalis'') | date = 23 September 2025 | publisher = In Our Nature | accessdate = 9 July 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://choosenatives.org/articles/plant-native-ground-covers-make-america-green/ | title = Plant Native Groundcovers and Make American Green Again | date = 20 April 2021 | publisher = Choose Natives! Promoting Native Plants in the Mid-Atlantic | accessdate = 9 July 2026}}</ref>
